atv2-b5-p1.transcript: Crown rot, and how far it travels. We ran spore samplers out from infected stands, and by distance it made no sense. Plots a few hundred metres out caught as much as the far ones. One five-kilometre plot out-caught everything inside it. Deverow predicted a peak at middling range; the middling plots caught least of the lot. Sort that catch by collector height and it lines up: tall masts caught heavily wherever they stood. We measured our hardware. Hedravean. Its harvest books run back a hundred and twenty years, and their bad years let us date outbreaks nobody recorded as disease. Managed ground, yes, but nobody has ever counted its trees — no population to calibrate against. Its growers spray about as often as the foresters. And we went to them: six years in before a grower wrote to us. Moving north? Ferrow says the northern records track our new sites. But those northern stands were surveyed clean twice before, and it is in them now. I credit the spread. Hallick reads the records as movement up the river valleys; the new finds sit north of the valleys' heads. The old southern specimens went back under the microscope — they are the same fungus. Next season, the edges. Our collectors have sat well inside the plots. The spore season shuts down by October, so autumn stays our stopping point. The cartridge readers do more, granted, but want mains power; our plots are an hour's walk from the nearest road. A gauge at each collector would be duplication, not data: rain we already log, from the met station beside plot four.

explanations.q1: Sorted by distance the samplers gave no pattern; sorted by mast height the catch lines up, which is why the professor says they measured their own hardware rather than the spore cloud.
explanations.q2: Hedravean earns its place for its harvest books running back a hundred and twenty years, whose bad years let the team put dates on outbreaks that were never recorded as disease.
explanations.q3: She credits the northward spread because stands added in the north, surveyed clean twice before, are turning the fungus up now.
explanations.q4: The collectors have been sitting well inside the plots and the professor says next season goes to the edges.

q1.0: A short-range collapse is contradicted outright: plots a few hundred metres out "caught as much as the far ones".
q1.1: A slow thinning with distance cannot hold when one five-kilometre plot "out-caught everything inside it".
q1.2: Deverow predicted exactly this middling peak and was corrected by the data — "the middling plots caught least of the lot".

q2.0: No spray pressure separates orchard from forest; its growers “spray about as often as the foresters”.
q2.1: The calibration reading is granted and then withdrawn: it is managed ground, but "nobody has ever counted its trees".
q2.3: The timing runs the other way — the team were “six years in before a grower wrote to us”.

q3.0: Ferrow puts the sampling-artifact reading and the professor answers it: "those northern stands were surveyed clean twice before", and the fungus is in them now.
q3.2: Re-examination of the old southern material settled that question — "they are the same fungus".
q3.3: Hallick's valley version is answered by where the finds are: "the new finds sit north of the valleys' heads".

q4.0: Autumn stopping is kept, not changed: "the spore season shuts down by October", so that is where the season ends.
q4.1: The cartridge readers are credited and then ruled out on siting: they “want mains power” and the plots are “an hour’s walk from the nearest road”.
q4.3: Weather data is already in hand rather than something to add — "rain we already log, from the met station beside plot four".

atv2-b5-p2.transcript: Trelundy infirmary and its weighing scheme. The dispenser's ledger first: it is a costing book. Extra diet, coals, the man's own hours, priced week by week; the total ran heavy enough that the governors twice set the scheme down for debate, and twice let it stand. Occupancy you get elsewhere: bed numbers come from the matron's returns. There are marginal notes, granted, haggling over the price of oatmeal. We date the break from the governors' minutes; the ledger runs unbroken through those years. The weighing itself. Physicians read the charts as a record of recovery. The ward staff had quite other ends in view: Friday's figures settled who could be put to work on the ward. The scale came in with a physician in the house's first month, and the kitchen inspections start twenty years later. Someone asked whether the balance was swapped — it was the same beam throughout. And the weighing did fix the shape of the week; true, though it is not my point. Maderwyn re-read the registers. Weight and length of stay track each other far more loosely than the reports of the day claimed. Winter and summer intakes gained at much the same rate. The gains scatter across quarter-ounces. The attendants' books disagree constantly rather than running alike. Rostrellick says the weighing shaped admission. His notes come from the eighteen sixties, a generation after the weighing began. Subscribers nominated, certainly, though the house physician struck names off the nomination lists. Until the admission registers are worked through, our papers cannot settle it — and I am withholding judgment on both ends.

explanations.q1: The ledger prices the diet, the coals and the dispenser's hours, and the professor's point is that the sum ran heavy enough that the governors twice set the scheme down for debate.
explanations.q2: The physicians took the charts as a record of recovery while the ward staff used Friday's figures for their own purpose — deciding who could be put to work.
explanations.q3: Maderwyn found weight and length of stay tracking each other loosely, far more loosely than contemporary reports claimed.
explanations.q4: He says the surviving papers cannot settle Rostrellick's claim until the admission registers are worked through, and he withholds judgment meanwhile.

q1.0: Occupancy is sourced elsewhere: "bed numbers come from the matron's returns".
q1.1: The marginal notes are granted and then narrowed to the wrong subject — they are "haggling over the price of oatmeal", not dosages.
q1.3: There is no gap to argue from: "the ledger runs unbroken through those years", and the break is dated from the minutes instead.

q2.0: The chronology reverses this origin story: the scale arrived in the house's first month, and "the kitchen inspections start twenty years later".
q2.2: A student raises the replaced-balance reading and is corrected — "it was the same beam throughout".
q2.3: The rhythm point is granted and set aside: the weighing "did fix the shape of the week", and that is not what interests him.

q3.0: The seasonal split is absent from her tables: "Winter and summer intakes gained at much the same rate".
q3.1: Rounding would show as clustering, and instead "The gains scatter across quarter-ounces".
q3.2: The independence question comes out the other way: "The attendants' books disagree constantly rather than running alike".

q4.0: The admission notes Rostrellick leans on are from the wrong period — "a generation after the weighing began".
q4.1: Subscriber control is conceded and then limited: subscribers nominated, but "the house physician struck names off the nomination lists".
q4.3: He does not settle for the retention version either; he says "I am withholding judgment on both ends".

atv2-b5-p3.transcript: Lanmorick priory. The survey of the eighteen forties first. Its measurements read as the restorers' job order: the bays to be underpinned are dimensioned to the inch, the roof they meant to strip is in section, the untouched north aisle gets one overall length. It records the intended works, and little besides. Marrable argues it was a pupils' exercise whose errors march in the order they worked; the surveyors were the contractor's own men, paid by the day out of the works account. Pennoy tells his students the field books beat the drawings made from them; the books hand the draughtsmen the same tidy figures. It did catch the south range that fell in eighteen fifty-one — in two lines and a width. The scan, now. The tower's cross-section comes out an oval, wider by a foot on the river face. It stands plumb to within a finger's breadth. Someone asked about the top stage: it sits true on the axis of the ones below. And the courses run level, rather than wavering as ground movement would leave them. Next, the roof spaces — the first campaign stopped at the wall heads — go up in the spring. Loading was settled last year by the engineers. Repeatability we tested at the outset, on the chapter house. The parish's other early buildings are a different grant and a different decade. The choir's mason's marks. Three-quarters sit in the two rebuilt bays, so they date the repairs rather than parcelling out the building seasons. The quarry marks are a separate alphabet. And the spacing wanders half a foot inside a single bay.

explanations.q1: The professor's main point is that the survey's measurements map the restorers' job order — detailed where works were planned, a single overall length where nothing was to be done.
explanations.q2: The scan showed the tower's cross-section to be an oval rather than a circle, wider by about a foot on the river face.
explanations.q3: The roof spaces, which the first campaign stopped short of at the wall heads, are what goes up in the spring.
explanations.q4: Three-quarters of the marks sit in the two rebuilt bays, which is what lets the team put a date to the repairs.

q1.1: Pennoy is the one who ranks the field books above the drawings, and the professor answers him: "the books hand the draughtsmen the same tidy figures".
q1.2: The accidental record is conceded and then cut down to almost nothing — the lost south range survives "in two lines and a width".
q1.3: Marrable's training-exercise reading meets a flat fact about who held the chain: the surveyors were "paid by the day out of the works account".

q2.0: A lean is incompatible with a tower that "stands plumb to within a finger's breadth".
q2.2: The off-axis reading is raised from the floor and corrected: the top stage "sits true on the axis of the ones below".
q2.3: Ground movement is contrasted away — "the courses run level, rather than wavering" as settlement would leave them.

q3.1: Structural work is done and behind them: "Loading was settled last year by the engineers".
q3.2: Repeatability belongs to an earlier stage and a different building — "Repeatability we tested at the outset, on the chapter house".
q3.3: The comparison campaign is granted but pushed off: the other early buildings are "a different grant and a different decade".

q4.0: The professor states the alternative explicitly: the marks "date the repairs rather than parcelling out the building seasons".
q4.2: The quarry link is raised and dismissed on the evidence — "The quarry marks are a separate alphabet".
q4.3: As a metrological check the marks are conceded useless: “the spacing wanders half a foot inside a single bay”.

atv2-b5-p4.transcript: The Dunmere wordbook, issued in parts. Lensham reads the prefaces as replies to the reviewers. I part company with her. Beside the subscription lists they are aimed at the people paying: thanks for patience, promises about the next part, apologies for the price. The first preface already names its subscribers, forty of them, before any notice appeared. The passages Lensham matches were in print before the reviews she pairs them with. The staff, meanwhile, got their instructions on printed slips, weekly. The archive is being catalogued. When that is done we shall see how the labour was shared out: each editor marked the material in his own ink, and those marks are on the slips still. Cut entries went with the proofs, and the proofs were pulped. The packets were opened by a clerk who kept the slips and burned the wrappers. The chief editor's annotated rival sits in a private collection in Dunmere. One entry to dwell on: a dialect name for a fishing float. It went to proof, then was pulled and reset — a second pass its neighbours were spared. Its evidence came in from four counties. You will read that its definition survives in six drafts; one draft survives, and a fair copy. Its etymology was wrong, and corrected in the second printing. Last, the slip recount. The collection grew fastest in the very years the annual reports call lean. The boxes for the commonest words are the fattest in the run. For the late letters the published figures run under the true holdings. And the misfiled slips are from the last decade of collecting.

explanations.q1: She disputes Lensham: read beside the subscription lists, the prefaces are aimed at the paying subscribers, thanking them for patience and apologising for the price.
explanations.q2: Once the archive is catalogued, the personal marks each editor left on the slips will show how the labour was shared out.
explanations.q3: The float entry went to proof and was then pulled and reset, taking a second pass that its neighbours were spared.
explanations.q4: The recount showed the collection growing fastest in the very years the annual reports describe as lean.

q1.0: The dating defeats the match: "The passages Lensham matches were in print before the reviews she pairs them with".
q1.2: There is no shift partway through — "The first preface already names its subscribers", before any notice had appeared.
q1.3: The staff had their own channel: they "got their instructions on printed slips, weekly".

q2.1: The cut material did not survive to be recovered: "Cut entries went with the proofs, and the proofs were pulped".
q2.2: The postmarks are gone — the clerk "kept the slips and burned the wrappers".
q2.3: The annotated rival is granted to exist but sits outside this archive, "in a private collection in Dunmere".

q3.0: No single-county problem arises: "Its evidence came in from four counties".
q3.1: The six-drafts claim is stated and corrected on the spot — "one draft survives, and a fair copy".
q3.2: The etymological error was short-lived, "corrected in the second printing", not carried through four.

q4.0: Thinning would have left those boxes light, and "The boxes for the commonest words are the fattest in the run".
q4.1: The error runs the other way: "the published figures run under the true holdings" for the late letters.
q4.2: The misfiling is granted but belongs to the wrong material — "the misfiled slips are from the last decade of collecting".

atv2-b5-p5.transcript:
The Trevoggan gorge salamanders — eleven seasons, and what the survey has measured.

Identification first. We have tagged these animals since the start; the tags come out of the budget after this season. What replaces them is a photograph, taken in the hand and matched by software against the spot pattern. Someone asked whether the adults would still be tagged. They won't — the camera treats an adult and a first-year alike.

The recapture figures. Estimates from the spring sessions ran well above the autumn ones for the same reach. We have run the same forty trap-nights a session since the third year, and both ends of the valley rise and fall together. A dozen did reappear within days of release, sooner than the model allows; too few to move the model.

So what have we measured? Mostly ourselves. Three stretches near the road supply the bulk of the detections, and those are the stretches we like walking. Weather counts, I grant you — a warm wet night doubles what enters a trap — but that washes out across a season, and our footpaths do not. Sort the catch by size and the same proportions come back each year. Hanwolla, before me, wrote that the animals shuttle onto the slopes in dry years; the slope transects came back with a handful of animals whatever the weather.

Polgrenna's second breeding site. Eggs turn up in the known pools a fortnight before the first young appear, in wet years and dry ones alike. The young come in one short pulse, ten days and done, and the pulse falls in the low-water weeks.

explanations.q1: The tags are being dropped and identification moves to the spot pattern: "the tags come out of the budget after this season", and what replaces them is a photograph matched by software against each animal's markings.
explanations.q2: The professor says estimates built from the spring sessions "ran well above the autumn ones for the same reach" — a within-year swing in the same stretch of water.
explanations.q3: His central claim is that the survey has measured the observers: "Three stretches near the road supply the bulk of the detections, and those are the stretches we like walking."
explanations.q4: He resists Polgrenna because the arrivals are concentrated: "The young come in one short pulse, ten days and done" — not the smeared arrival a second source would give.

q1.1: Running tags and photographs on together is closed off by a positive statement of the budget: "the tags come out of the budget after this season".
q1.2: A student raises exactly this option and is corrected — the adults go untagged too, since "the camera treats an adult and a first-year alike".
q1.3: The replacement still involves handling, so a distance-read tag is not what is coming: the photograph is "taken in the hand and matched by software".

q2.1: The premise of a cut in effort is false for this survey: "the same forty trap-nights a session since the third year".
q2.2: Early reappearances are granted and then restricted to nothing: "too few to move the model".
q2.3: The two ends are not independent — they "rise and fall together".

q3.0: Trappability with weather is conceded and then narrowed out of the answer: a warm wet night doubles the catch, "but that washes out across a season, and our footpaths do not".
q3.1: A decline in the large size classes would show as a change of composition, and there is none: "Sort the catch by size and the same proportions come back each year."
q3.3: This was Hanwolla's published reading and the professor corrects it: "the slope transects came back with a handful of animals whatever the weather".

q4.0: The order of appearance runs the other way — eggs "turn up in the known pools a fortnight before the first young appear".
q4.1: There is no wet-year/dry-year split to hang it on, since the same pattern holds "in wet years and dry ones alike".
q4.2: Transport in a spate is incompatible with the timing he gives: "the pulse falls in the low-water weeks".

atv2-b5-p6.transcript:
Morgelly's studio ledger — Threlmoor, thirty years of sittings.

Pricing first. Across the square, Ivestead charged one fee for the sitting however many prints went out; Morgelly charged by the print. Ivestead's sitting stood a shilling below Morgelly's, and a group paid that same shilling again. His fee rose twice in twenty years, both times when he took larger premises. One of you had read that he discounted for regulars. His book gives the same figure for a stranger and for a man on his fourth sitting.

Chelvern says the ledger was written up afterwards, for show. I don't accept it. The ink shifts from entry to entry, the way a book kept daily will; the hand is his throughout, which tells us who wrote it, not when. The earliest volume shows the same ink shifts as the later ones. So: not an open question but a settled one — the ink changes at the entry.

Now, the plate makers' price lists. His exposures hold at about the same length right through the change of plates, and his invoices are bound into the back of the same ledger. The interest is not what he bought but what he sold on: the counter trade in plates and chemicals brought him more than the camera work did.

Which leaves the light. The handbook figures reach his pages a good decade after the journals printed them. He opens up a stop for children; past that, the settings answer the sky. It won't date his prints — half the sittings go unnamed — but knowing his habits, it reads as an instrument.

explanations.q1: The rival is used to make the contrast in pricing structure: Ivestead "charged one fee for the sitting however many prints went out", where Morgelly charged by the print.
explanations.q2: She rejects Chelvern outright, and her evidence is the ink: "The ink shifts from entry to entry, the way a book kept daily will."
explanations.q3: The plate makers' lists let her price his side trade, and she concludes the "counter trade in plates and chemicals brought him more than the camera work did".
explanations.q4: Her central point is that the ledger records his own judgment of light and can be used as an instrument: "once you know his habits, it reads as an instrument".

q1.1: His group charge is stated as the same single fee, and his sitting fee is given as below Morgelly's rather than level with it: it "stood a shilling below Morgelly's".
q1.2: The rises are granted and then attributed elsewhere: his fee rose twice in twenty years, "both times when he took larger premises".
q1.3: A student reports the discounting story and the professor corrects it from the books, which give "the same figure for a stranger and for a man on his fourth sitting".

q2.1: The uniform hand is granted and then restricted so it cannot carry the argument: it "tells us who wrote it, not when".
q2.2: The earliest volume is covered by the same evidence as the rest — it "shows the same ink shifts as the later ones".
q2.3: She treats the question as decided, "not an open question but a settled one".

q3.0: Exposure times do not move with the plates: they "hold at about the same length right through the change of plates".
q3.1: The comparison is drawn on the selling side, not the buying side: "The interest is not what he bought but what he sold on".
q3.3: His purchase papers do survive — the "invoices are bound into the back of the same ledger".

q4.1: He is behind the press rather than ahead of it: the handbook figures reach his pages "a good decade after the journals printed them".
q4.2: The sitter's effect is granted for children and then shut down: past that, "the settings answer the sky".
q4.3: It cannot serve as a dating tool, since "half the sittings go unnamed".

atv2-b5-p7.transcript:
The measured mile off Aberwynt. In eighteen ninety-four a coal company put a pier across the sight line from the northern beacon, and the course had to be shifted a mile down the coast and surveyed afresh. The navy paid for the beacons and the navy paid to move them. Porthlenny's figures do sit a touch high, but the two grounds were surveyed to one standard and convert cleanly. And the timings came off the ship's own stopwatches, not from the shore huts.

Now, the yard papers, catalogued last winter. What I expect from them is the post survey: how far the marker posts had drifted from the distance the charts gave them. The Penvorran's propellers are in her completion book — the pair she carried into service. Her draught was read off the marks that morning and both sides signed for it. And the sister ship was six months from launching.

Nansveor charges the fleet with inflating trial speeds. I go part way with him. The export figures run high, by a knot and a half, and that was not an error in the current allowance but a decision taken ashore. The home trials come out straight, year after year.

Coal returns, finally. Ships tried in the winter months returned higher figures than those tried in summer. One of you suggested the stokers: sort the returns by stokehold and they scatter less than they do by ship. Trial-day burning sits above what the same ships used on passage. Two yards did return in bushels, and the clerk converted those before the tables were made up.

explanations.q1: The mile is described to trace a forced relocation: a coal company's pier blocked the sight line, so "the course had to be shifted a mile down the coast and surveyed afresh".
explanations.q2: He expects the yard papers to settle the geometry of the course: "how far the marker posts had drifted from the distance the charts gave them".
explanations.q3: He splits the charge by market: "The export figures run high", while "The home trials come out straight, year after year."
explanations.q4: The survey showed a seasonal difference: "Ships tried in the winter months returned higher figures than those tried in summer."

q1.0: Upkeep is placed with the service, not the port: "The navy paid for the beacons and the navy paid to move them."
q1.1: The comparison problem is conceded in part and then dismissed — the two grounds "were surveyed to one standard and convert cleanly".
q1.2: The timings have a different source altogether: they "came off the ship's own stopwatches, not from the shore huts".

q2.1: The propeller question is already answered elsewhere and the professor says so: her propellers are in her completion book, "the pair she carried into service".
q2.2: Nothing private is left to recover about the draught, which "was read off the marks that morning and both sides signed for it".
q2.3: A rehearsal with the sister ship was not available at that date — she "was six months from launching".

q3.0: He locates the excess in intent rather than in arithmetic: it "was not an error in the current allowance but a decision taken ashore".
q3.1: The charge is limited to the export orders; the domestic runs stay clean over the period, since the home trials "come out straight, year after year".
q3.2: The direction of the error is upward: the export figures "run high, by a knot and a half".

q4.0: A student proposes the crews and the professor corrects it with the sort: "sort the returns by stokehold and they scatter less than they do by ship".
q4.1: Trial-day burning is placed above ordinary steaming, not below: it "sits above what the same ships used on passage".
q4.3: The measures were granted as different and then reconciled: "the clerk converted those before the tables were made up".

atv2-b5-p8.transcript:
The Marnstow estuary: the silt record, and what we do next.

Here is the claim: the shoaling follows the works along the banks far more closely than anything the river brings down. Each training wall shows in the soundings inside three years of being built, and the mean depth at the bar changed by six feet inside forty years. The board did add stations where it wanted a case, I grant that; drop those stations and the pattern stands.

What next? We core the three reaches the series marks as gaining fastest, to see whether the mud agrees. Not further back into the paper — the older harbour charts can wait. The raw sounding books are already on the shelf at the record office. And the lead line was run beside modern gear in the seventies; they agree to a few inches.

Ordwell's replotting. He expected the deep water to have crept toward the town shore, and said so in his first paper; his replot put it back where the charts had it. What he found instead: after each dredging the channel fills quickest through the first winter, then slackens off. Two stations had moved between crews, and Ordwell renamed them before plotting. The monthly gauge shows shoals sitting put for years at a time.

Why Fenrith? The ferry keeper's own depth notes cover the years the official series leaves blank. The slip was rebuilt at some point — the parish argued for years about which year. The silting suit came sixty years after the gap. And that painting in the town hall: the tide in it is anyone's guess.

explanations.q1: He implies a coring campaign aimed at the fastest-shoaling reaches: they will "core the three reaches the series marks as gaining fastest".
explanations.q2: His central claim ties the shoaling to the bank works: it "follows the works along the banks far more closely than anything the river brings down".
explanations.q3: Ordwell found a decay curve in the refilling: "after each dredging the channel fills quickest through the first winter, then slackens off".
explanations.q4: Fenrith matters for the keeper's private notes, which "cover the years the official series leaves blank".

q1.0: The next move is explicitly toward the sediment rather than the archive: "Not further back into the paper — the older harbour charts can wait."
q1.1: Publication is granted little point because the raw books "are already on the shelf at the record office".
q1.2: That instrument comparison belongs to an earlier decade and is settled: run in the seventies, "they agree to a few inches".

q2.1: The board's self-serving station choice is conceded and then neutralized: "drop those stations and the pattern stands".
q2.2: The response time is short enough for one engineer to see: each training wall shows "inside three years of being built".
q2.3: A quiet estuary is incompatible with the figures given — the mean depth at the bar "changed by six feet inside forty years".

q3.0: This was Ordwell's own expectation and his replot corrected it: it "put it back where the charts had it".
q3.1: The moved stations are granted and then handled, since "Ordwell renamed them before plotting".
q3.2: Shoals are described as persistent rather than short-lived: the monthly gauge shows them "sitting put for years at a time".

q4.1: The rebuilding supplies no firm date, since "the parish argued for years about which year".
q4.2: The testimony falls outside the period at issue: "The silting suit came sixty years after the gap."
q4.3: The painting fails as a check on water level: "the tide in it is anyone's guess".
